title: Procedural Generation
blurb: Grow caves, rooms, terrain, names and loot from a single seed number, and get the exact same world every time.
intro:
Procedural generation means letting code build your content: dungeons, caves, terrain, loot, even names. Minecraft worlds, Spelunky levels and roguelike dungeons all come from it.

The secret ingredient is a seeded random number generator. Give it the same seed and it produces the same "random" numbers every time, so a seed like 1234 always builds the same world. That's how players share seeds, and it's how the checks here can test your code.

Each starter includes a small generator called mulberry32. You don't need to understand its insides. You just call it with a seed and it hands you a function that returns a new number from 0 up to (but not including) 1 each time you call it.

Tip

Godot's RandomNumberGenerator has a seed property, and GameMaker has random_set_seed(). Same idea, built in.
links: Red Blob Games: Noise functions and map generation

stages.l:
Math.random() gives a different number every time you run your program. That's great for a dice roll, but terrible if you want to share a cool level with a friend, or test your code.

A seeded generator fixes that. You make one with a seed, then call it again and again for the next number in its sequence:

const rand = mulberry32(42);
rand();   // 0.6011...
rand();   // 0.4482...
const again = mulberry32(42);
again();  // 0.6011... the same as before!

Same seed, same sequence. Different seed, different sequence.
stages.p: Make a generator from seed and return an array of its first n numbers.
stages.h: const rand = mulberry32(seed); then loop n times, pushing rand() into an array.

stages.l:
rand() gives a decimal from 0 up to 1. To get a whole number from min to max (both included):

Math.floor(rand() * (max - min + 1)) + min

Why it works for a six-sided die (min = 1, max = 6):

  • rand() * 6 is somewhere from 0 to 5.999...
  • Math.floor chops it to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5
  • + 1 shifts it to 1 to 6
stages.p: Return an array of count whole numbers from min to max, using a generator made from seed.
stages.h: Inside a loop: out.push(Math.floor(rand() * (max - min + 1)) + min);

stages.l:
To pick a random item, pick a random index from 0 to list.length - 1. From now on the starter includes a randInt(rand, min, max) helper that does the formula from the last stage.

const rand = mulberry32(7);
const enemies = ["slime", "bat", "orc"];
const e = enemies[randInt(rand, 0, enemies.length - 1)];
stages.p: Return an array of n random picks from list (the same item can come up more than once).
stages.h: Loop n times and push list[randInt(rand, 0, list.length - 1)].

stages.l:
Real loot isn't evenly random: coins should drop often and crowns rarely. A loot table gives each item a weight. Bigger weight, more common.

The trick: roll a number from 0 up to the total weight, then walk down the table subtracting weights until the roll fits.

// table: [["coin", 70], ["gem", 25], ["crown", 5]]  total 100
let r = rand() * 100;       // say r is 82
// 82 < 70? no.  r = 82 - 70 = 12
// 12 < 25? yes! it's a gem
stages.p: table is a list of [item, weight] pairs. Return an array of n items rolled from it. For each roll use exactly one rand(): let r = rand() * total;, then check each pair in order.
stages.h: Work out total first. Then for each roll: loop over the pairs, if (r < weight) that's your item, otherwise r -= weight;

stages.l:
Shuffling a deck of cards, the order of enemy waves, a playlist: you need a fair shuffle. The classic one is Fisher-Yates. Walk backwards through the array and swap each spot with a random spot at or before it.

for (let i = a.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {
  const j = randInt(rand, 0, i);
  [a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]];   // swap
}
Tip

[a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]] swaps two items in one line using destructuring.
stages.p: Return a shuffled copy of arr using Fisher-Yates exactly as in the example. Don't change arr itself.
stages.h: Copy first with const a = arr.slice(); then run the loop on a and return it.

stages.l:
A random walk takes one step in a random direction, again and again. It's the starting point for wandering monsters, rivers, and the cave carver in the next stages.

const DIRS = [[1, 0], [-1, 0], [0, 1], [0, -1]];   // right, left, down, up
const [dx, dy] = DIRS[randInt(rand, 0, 3)];
x += dx;
y += dy;
stages.p: Start at [0, 0]. Take steps steps, choosing each direction with DIRS[randInt(rand, 0, 3)] using the DIRS order above. Return every position visited as [x, y] pairs, including the start.
stages.h: Start the path as [[0, 0]]. After each step, push [x, y]. You should end up with steps + 1 positions.

stages.l:
Most generators work on a grid of tiles. An array of arrays is easy to change: grid[y][x] is the tile in row y, column x. To print it or compare it, join each row into a string.

const grid = [];
for (let y = 0; y < 2; y++) grid.push(new Array(4).fill("#"));
grid[1][2] = ".";
console.log(grid.map(row => row.join("")));
["####", "##.#"]

We'll use # for walls and . for floor.
stages.p: Build a grid w tiles wide and h tiles tall, filled with #, and return it as an array of strings.
stages.h: Loop h times and push new Array(w).fill("#"), then return grid.map(row => row.join(""));

stages.l:
Combine the last two ideas and you get a cave! The drunkard's walk starts in the middle of a solid map and stumbles around, carving floor wherever it steps.

To keep a solid border, the walker isn't allowed onto the outer ring of tiles. If a step would take it there, it stays where it is for that step.

const nx = x + dx, ny = y + dy;
if (nx >= 1 && nx <= w - 2 && ny >= 1 && ny <= h - 2) {
  x = nx;
  y = ny;
}
grid[y][x] = ".";
stages.p: Fill a w by h grid with #. Start at x = Math.floor(w / 2), y = Math.floor(h / 2) and carve it. Then steps times: pick a direction with DIRS[randInt(rand, 0, 3)], move if allowed, and carve. Return the rows as strings.
stages.h: Carve the start before the loop. Inside the loop, carve after the move check, even if the walker didn't move.

stages.l:
Another way to make caves starts with pure noise: every tile is randomly a wall or a floor. It looks like TV static at first. The next two stages turn that static into smooth caves.

grid[y][x] = rand() < 0.45 ? "#" : ".";   // about 45% walls

The order you visit tiles matters with a seeded generator, because each tile uses the next number in the sequence.
stages.p: Build a w by h grid, row by row from the top, left to right. Each tile is # if rand() < fill, otherwise .. Return the rows as strings.
stages.h: Two loops, y outside and x inside. Build each row as a string with row += rand() < fill ? "#" : ".";

stages.l:
Cave smoothing needs to know how many of a tile's 8 neighbours are walls. Two nested loops from -1 to 1 visit them all; skip the middle one, which is the tile itself.

for (let dy = -1; dy <= 1; dy++) {
  for (let dx = -1; dx <= 1; dx++) {
    if (dx === 0 && dy === 0) continue;
    // look at grid[y + dy][x + dx]
  }
}

Tiles outside the map count as walls. That keeps caves closed at the edges. Careful: grid[-1] is undefined, so check the row exists before reading from it.
stages.p: grid is an array of strings. Return how many of the 8 tiles around (x, y) are walls, counting anything outside the grid as a wall.
stages.h: const row = grid[y + dy]; then count it if row === undefined || row[x + dx] === undefined || row[x + dx] === "#"

stages.l:
Cellular automata sounds fancy, but it's a simple rule applied to every tile at once. For caves, each tile looks at its neighbours:

  • 5 or more walls around it: it becomes a wall
  • 3 or fewer: it becomes floor
  • exactly 4: it stays as it was

Run that once or twice on random noise and the static clumps into natural-looking caves.

Tip

Build a new grid and read only from the old one. If you change tiles as you go, later tiles see a half-updated map and the result goes lopsided.
stages.p: Return a new grid (array of strings) after one smoothing step using the rule above. The starter includes countWalls from the last stage.
stages.h: For each tile: const n = countWalls(grid, x, y); then n >= 5 ? "#" : n <= 3 ? "." : grid[y][x]

stages.l:
Dungeon generators place rectangular rooms, and two rooms mustn't overlap. A room is { x, y, w, h }: its top-left tile and its size. Two rectangles overlap when they overlap on both axes:

a.x < b.x + b.w &&   // a starts before b ends (horizontally)
b.x < a.x + a.w &&   // b starts before a ends
a.y < b.y + b.h &&   // same two checks, vertically
b.y < a.y + a.h

Rooms that only touch edges don't count as overlapping. This check is called AABB (axis-aligned bounding box) and it's the most common collision test in 2D games.
stages.p: Return true if rooms a and b overlap.
stages.h: Return all four checks joined with &&.

stages.l:
The simplest room placer just tries: make a random room, and keep it only if it doesn't hit any room you already have. After enough tries, the map fills up.

To leave at least one wall tile between rooms, test against a grown copy of each existing room:

const grown = { x: r.x - 1, y: r.y - 1, w: r.w + 2, h: r.h + 2 };
stages.p: Repeat tries times. Each try, roll in exactly this order: rw = randInt(rand, 3, 6), rh = randInt(rand, 3, 5), x = randInt(rand, 1, w - rw - 1), y = randInt(rand, 1, h - rh - 1). Keep the room { x, y, w: rw, h: rh } if it doesn't overlap the grown copy of any kept room. Return the kept rooms.
stages.h: Use rooms.some(r => roomsOverlap(room, { x: r.x - 1, y: r.y - 1, w: r.w + 2, h: r.h + 2 })) to test for a clash. Roll all four numbers every try, even ones that get thrown away.

stages.l:
Rooms need joining up. The easiest corridor is an L shape: go sideways until you line up with the target, then go straight up or down.

// from [1, 1] to [4, 3]
// sideways: [1,1] [2,1] [3,1] [4,1]
// then down:              [4,2] [4,3]

Math.sign(to - from) gives 1, -1 or 0: the direction to step in.
stages.p: from and to are [x, y]. Return every tile of the corridor in order: first along x at from's row, then along y at to's column. Include both ends, and don't list the corner twice.
stages.h: Start with let x = from[0], y = from[1]; const tiles = [[x, y]]; While x !== to[0], step x and push. Then while y !== to[1], step y and push.

stages.l:
Pure random heights make spiky, ugly hills. Value noise is smoother: pick random values only every few steps (the key points), then lerp between them to fill the gaps.

// spacing 4: random keys at 0, 4, 8...
const k = Math.floor(i / spacing);    // key to the left
const t = (i % spacing) / spacing;    // how far toward the next key
const v = keys[k] + (keys[k + 1] - keys[k]) * t;

Stack a few layers of this at different spacings and you get the hills of a side-scroller.
stages.p: First roll Math.floor((length - 1) / spacing) + 2 key values with rand(). Then return an array of length values using the lerp from the example.
stages.h: Make the keys array first in its own loop. Then loop i from 0 to length - 1 and push the lerped value.

stages.l:
Another way to calm down bumpy terrain is a moving average: replace each height with the average of itself and its neighbours. Peaks get lower, dips get filled in.

// [0, 9, 0]
// first:  (0 + 9) / 2      = 4.5   (no left neighbour)
// middle: (0 + 9 + 0) / 3  = 3
// last:   (9 + 0) / 2      = 4.5
stages.p: Return a new array where each height is the average of itself and whichever of its left and right neighbours exist.
stages.h: For each i, add up heights[i - 1], heights[i] and heights[i + 1] when they're not undefined, and count how many you added.

stages.l:
Now draw it! A side-view world like Terraria turns each column's height into a stack of ground tiles. Row 0 is the top of the screen, so a tile at row y is ground when the column is tall enough to reach it:

// heights [1, 3, 2], rows 3
// row 0 needs height 3:  .#.
// row 1 needs height 2:  .##
// row 2 needs height 1:  ###

In general, the tile at row y is ground if heights[i] >= rows - y.

Tip

To turn heights into biomes instead, map ranges to tiles: low is water, middle is grass, high is mountain.
stages.p: Return rows strings, top row first. Each string has one character per height: # for ground, . for sky.
stages.h: For each y from 0 to rows - 1: heights.map(hh => hh >= rows - y ? "#" : ".").join("")

stages.l:
Glue random syllables together and you get fantasy names for towns, planets and NPCs. Pick each syllable from a list, join them, and give the result a capital letter.

const name = "korami";
name[0].toUpperCase() + name.slice(1);   // "Korami"
stages.p: Pick count syllables, each with syllables[randInt(rand, 0, syllables.length - 1)]. Join them and return the name with its first letter in capitals.
stages.h: Build a string in a loop, then return name[0].toUpperCase() + name.slice(1);

stages.l:
Pure random dice can roll five 1s in a row, which feels unfair. Some board games and puzzle games use a bag instead: put one of each face in a bag, shuffle it, and draw. When the bag is empty, refill it and shuffle again. Every face comes up exactly once per bag. Tetris uses this for its pieces!

if (bag.length === 0) {
  bag = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
  // shuffle bag with Fisher-Yates
}
const roll = bag.shift();   // take from the front
stages.p: Return n draws from a six-sided dice bag. Refill with [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] whenever the bag is empty, shuffle with Fisher-Yates exactly like the shuffle stage, and draw from the front.
stages.h: Fisher-Yates: for (let i = bag.length - 1; i > 0; i--) { const j = randInt(rand, 0, i); [bag[i], bag[j]] = [bag[j], bag[i]]; }

stages.l:
Time to build a whole dungeon from one seed. You've written every piece already; now chain them:

  • Place rooms with 30 tries, exactly like the placing rooms stage.
  • Start with a w by h grid of # and carve every tile of every room to ..
  • Each room's centre is [room.x + Math.floor(room.w / 2), room.y + Math.floor(room.h / 2)].
  • Join each room to the one before it with an L-shaped corridor between their centres, carving those tiles too.

Then summarise what you made, so the game can show it on a loading screen.

Tip

Paste in your roomsOverlap and corridor functions from earlier stages. Reusing small, tested helpers is how real generators are built.
stages.p: Return { rooms, floor, start, exit, map }: the number of rooms, how many . tiles the map has, the centre of the first room, the centre of the last room, and the map as an array of strings.
stages.h: Use one rand for everything. Count floor tiles at the end with map.join("").split(".").length - 1, or loop and count.
